name: Dive Deep
definition: Leaders operate at all levels, stay connected to the details, audit frequently, and are skeptical when metrics and anecdote differ. No task is beneath them.

rows.situation: When reviewing contribution or unit economics
rows.under: Looks at the category total against last year and never drills into product line, supplier, or cost component.
rows.justRight: Reviews the top and bottom product lines on a useful cadence, splits contribution into components (for example, shipping cost), and names both the unit-level actions and the root-cause problem (for example, supplier funding missing on every product from that supplier).
rows.over: Daily analysis of the top 1,000 contributors by every component, with a request for the state of each product. The report takes most of the day and leaves no time to fix anything.

rows.situation: When data is presented in a review
rows.under: Takes every number at face value. Does not ask how it was built, or whether it is agenda-free.
rows.justRight: Challenges how the number was derived, probes outliers, and tests both the data and the presenter's reading of it.
rows.over: Derails the meeting by asking for the same data cut twelve ways, with no story for how the next cut would change the decision.

rows.situation: When a key metric looks wrong
rows.under: Treats the unusual number as weather and waits until the business is already hurt.
rows.justRight: Forms a hypothesis, finds the root cause, and puts a preventative fix in place so the same problem does not return.
rows.over: Spins up a crowd and a week of work for a blip with almost no business impact.

rows.situation: When a program beats the plan
rows.under: Enjoys the good week and learns nothing.
rows.justRight: Studies why it worked, then doubles down and replicates the principle wherever it holds.
rows.over: Spends the win investigating why last year was bad, because that is what made this year look good, and never uses the time to scale what is working.

rows.situation: When the work needs another pair of hands
rows.under: Unwilling to step in. Treats the messy task as beneath them.
rows.justRight: Rolls up sleeves when the owner is stuck, follows through, and then hands the work back.
rows.over: Jumps in at the slightest deviation and stifles ownership and invention.

rows.situation: When staying connected to the work
rows.under: Delegates and only talks to the immediate team.
rows.justRight: Stays connected at every level: walks the floor, talks to people who do the work, and still works through the people who lead them.
rows.over: Works several levels down and changes direction without telling the leaders in between.

rows.under: Treats metrics as a high-level weather report and never learns the drivers.
rows.justRight: Knows the underlying drivers, how they have trended, and who owns each one.
rows.over: Lives in the minutiae, loses the larger picture, and uses the data pile as a substitute for a decision.

rows.under: Fixes the symptom. Always delegates the question. Cannot describe the cause in one sentence.
rows.justRight: Reviews the metrics, asks why until the cause is specific, and then decides.
rows.over: Analysis paralysis. No decision, and no delegation.

rows.situation: When a business case or variance lands on the desk
rows.under: Skips due diligence. Accepts the projection and creates a controllership risk.
rows.justRight: Does enough work to find the blind spots, then improves the proposal so the company is better off.
rows.over: Asks for irrelevant detail, blocks momentum, and micromanages the author.

rows.situation: When making a claim in a room
rows.under: Leads with I think. Blames other teams without data. Stays high-level and fakes fluency.
rows.justRight: Can get to the supporting fact, or to the person who has it, quickly. Calls a detail only when it changes something larger. Does not fake it.
rows.over: Drills every cell with no sense of what matters. Berates people who cannot produce a trivia answer on the spot.
